Wall Street’s “fear gauges” just had their biggest day in years. So what normally happens next?

The VIX jumped 69.7% to 28.17 Thursday, its biggest one-day gain since December 2024 and second-largest since the February 2018 “Volmageddon,” per Cboe. It was also its highest close since March 30.

The VVIX (the VIX of the VIX) rose 49.3% to 134.99, its biggest one-day gain since February 2007 and its biggest point gain since Volmageddon. So traders weren’t just hedging against further stock declines, they were scrambling to hedge volatility itself.

What history says (calculations from Cboe data):
▪️ VIX up 60%+ in a day (5 prior cases since 1990): S&P 500 higher a month later all 5 times
▪️ VIX up 40%+ (24 cases): higher a month later 18 times, and a year later 22 times, by an average of almost 19%
▪️ VIX up 40%+ and VVIX up 30%+ the same day (6 cases since 2007): higher a month later every time, but a year later only 4 of 6, averaging about 4%

Big caveat with the small sample sizes, and note it can be just the start of something much bigger, like February 2020, when the S&P was down 24% a month later. 

Getting more granular, spikes from a calm base like this one have had weaker three-month follow-through. And the closest match for both gauges, February 27, 2007, saw the S&P slightly lower a year later.

Something I have been writing about at @RealVision in past months: there was too much leverage in US equities. Opportunities will present in the coming weeks and months, but here was the breakdown from my reports. 
---------------------
Margin debt is 6.3% of M2 and 4.5% of GDP, near record highs. Relative to household equity and US stock market cap, it's less stretched, but the real story is the rate of change. All of them hit more than +2 standard deviations above their 4-year norms.

As always, the stock of debt isn't the trigger. The speed of it is.

🧵

The setup is when 3-month annualised margin debt growth crosses +100%. Confirmation is when it then turns negative.

In 2000, 2007 and 2021 that sequence was followed by S&P 500 drawdowns of 15% to 48% within two years. 2004 was the dud.

September just confirmed: -5.7%. The trend is still holding, so this is the warning, not the break.

A market this levered is looking for an excuse. AI isn't going anywhere, but the payoff is slower than priced and growth is slowing.

A reset in prices will set up incredible buying, but first we need to see if it goes systemic and spills into credit. That's when the authorities really take notice.

My Liquidity Stress Indicator is elevated (not the best environment for $BTC returns) but not extreme, and it's cooled in recent days. Watch the SOFR-IORB spread though. It's creeping up again.https://t.co/maQWvVsch2

We know what the response will be if repo markets freeze up, IG spreads widen too fast and equities fall 20%.

I've been pointing to a low in the liquidity cycle around Q1 next year. All signs point that way, possibly earlier depending on how bad this deleveraging gets. Only Bessent and co know when they'll step in.

And while Bitcoin's sensitivity to global liquidity has been falling, it shines during big policy shifts. We saw that in August, when price inflected off a small buyback announcement (more signal than substance).
